About 2 minutes. State the purpose plainly: Make It Count is a pilot, and Kaizen is continuing to develop. This school is helping us understand what is useful in real primary classrooms, what needs improvement and where the approach could work on a wider scale. Say: Your feedback will help shape both the professional-development programme and the software. We want specific examples of what works and what does not. This is a partnership in development, not a claim that the programme is already proven. Confirm Grades 4–6 and the school's priorities. Access is arranged; keep credentials off the shared screen. Programme status and feedback purpose supplied directly by Dr Megel Barker in this conversation.

About 2 minutes. Welcome the primary teachers and leadership team. Today focuses on mathematics teaching in Grades 4–6 and support for PEP preparation. Confirm which grades the participants teach. Ask: Which mathematical ideas or word problems do your pupils find hardest to explain? School login/access is already arranged. Keep passwords and school access codes off the shared screen. Do not promise PEP score gains. Presenter name and programme context come from Dr Megel Barker in this conversation.

About 2 minutes. Explain the three routes as alternatives for different teacher needs. Ask teachers to judge the fit: Can you find a suitable topic quickly? Is the language clear? Is the difficulty right? Would this save preparation time? Use primary topics and check each worksheet's content before selecting it for a class. Record missing resources and suggestions. Do not promise that every request will be implemented; explain that classroom feedback will help decide priorities.

About 2 minutes. Show the three existing Kaizen destinations. Teaching Tools: start with number, fractions of quantities, money, measurement, geometry or data, matching the class objective. For Grades 5–6, select percentage, ratio or reverse-reasoning examples only when pupils have covered them. Build a Worksheet lets the teacher choose question types and quantities. Ready-Made Resources provides quick topic sheets, but select by content and difficulty rather than using secondary exam collections as primary resources. For curriculum planning open https://www.kaizenmaths.com/#/curriculum-alignments/jamaica-nsc-4-6. The NSC mapping supports planning and does not guarantee that every item matches the latest assessment requirements. Source: app.js Jamaica NSC Grades 4–6 alignment and tools/pep-practice/index.html in the existing application.
A focused classroom demonstration
Kaizen Maths  /  Make It Count
LIVE DEMONSTRATION

1  Try a PEP-style question
2  Compare bar support and worked steps
3  Create or print a classroom resource

Where would this help your teaching?
What would you change?
www.kaizenmaths.com

Allow 8–10 minutes. Focus on three demonstrations rather than touring every feature.

1. PEP-style Practice (3 minutes): open https://www.kaizenmaths.com/#/tools/pep-practice . Choose Grade 4, 5 or 6 and one familiar skill, such as fractions of quantities, money, or area and perimeter. Click New practice. Keep Assessment-style selected. Let teachers attempt one item before revealing anything. Ask: Is the wording clear? Does this fit a topic your pupils are learning? The tool provides selected original classroom practice, not full official PEP coverage.

2. Teaching support (3 minutes): without generating a new set, switch the SAME questions to With bar-model support, then open Worked solutions & marks. Ask what the diagram makes clearer, what pupils might misread, and whether the steps need more detail. Bar modelling is our optional teaching scaffold, not a prescribed PEP response. Explain that later independent practice should remove the added scaffold. Avoid interpreting a supported response as an independent assessment result.

3. A resource for tomorrow (2 minutes): show Print / PDF, including Both question versions or Worked solutions only. If time remains, open https://www.kaizenmaths.com/#/worksheet-generator , add one primary topic block, show answers/worked steps and print preview. As a quick alternative, show a suitable primary topic sheet from Ready-Made Resources. Ask: Could you use this tomorrow? What would you change about the layout or controls?

End with 1–2 minutes for teachers to name one classroom use and one improvement. Note access, usability, content and teaching suggestions separately in your meeting notes. Keep logins off screen. Source: the existing tool controls in tools/pep-practice/index.html and the Kaizen navigation. Screenshot: output/resource-navigation-preview.png, an actual workspace screenshot. No feedback form or collection system is assumed by this deck.
Make It Count: learning together
Kaizen Maths  /  Make It Count
Bar modelling

Three quarters of a class is 18 pupils.
How many pupils are in the class?

What is the whole?
What does one equal part represent?

Tell us where the explanation helps pupils
and where it needs to change.

About 2 minutes. Use the example to model the kind of feedback we want about the professional development. The answer is 24 pupils: three equal parts total 18, so one part is 6 and four parts total 24. Ask teachers to identify the whole and explain one part before calculating. Then ask: Would this explanation help your pupils? Where might they get stuck? What language, prior examples or pacing would you change? Their experience should help shape how we teach the strategy, not just how the software looks. Invite alternative valid methods. Try a fresh unscaffolded problem later to explore whether understanding transfers.

About 2 minutes. Invite teachers to solve the class problem without support first. Three quarters is 18 pupils. Draw a whole as four equal parts: three parts together represent 18. One part is 18 ÷ 3 = 6. The whole is 4 × 6 = 24 pupils. Check that three quarters of 24 is 18. Ask what changes if a pupil divides 18 by 4: they have treated the known part as the whole. Discuss pupils' words as well as their numerical answer. In Make It Count, use bars to teach the structure, then give a fresh assessment-style problem without an added model to check independent understanding. Bar modelling is our chosen teaching scaffold. Do not present it as a mandated PEP response. Other mathematically valid strategies remain welcome. Grade-appropriate progression can include forward fractions before reverse fractions, then percentages, ratio and linked steps. Sources: assets/courses/bar-modelling-data.js and the teacher guidance in tools/pep-practice/index.html. Programme artwork remains the supplied Make It Count asset.

title: How the six-week pilot will work

text: How the six-week pilot will work
Kaizen Maths  /  Make It Count
Starting point
Agree a grade, an NSC objective and a teaching need.
Classroom use
Try a strategy and a Kaizen resource with pupils.
Teacher feedback
Share what helped, what was unclear and what is missing.
Next version
Use feedback to improve the programme and software.
Your experience will inform decisions about wider use.

About 2 minutes. Present the six-week structure as a proposed pilot, with actual dates and arrangements to agree. Begin with a grade, NSC objective and school teaching need. Teachers try the learning activities and software in class, share short examples, and help us identify changes worth making. We will use those observations to refine the programme and software and inform decisions about wider use. Be clear that feedback informs priorities; it does not guarantee every request or prove impact. Ask about usefulness, clarity, preparation time, classroom practicality, accessibility, pupil misconceptions and independent understanding. Confidence reflections before and after can support discussion, but do not establish that the pilot caused any change. Agree any research participation, consent and sharing of findings separately, and avoid identifying pupils. Confirm feedback arrangements with the school rather than implying that a form, survey or reporting feature already exists.

About 2 minutes. Keep this a proposed six-week programme; agree actual dates with the school. Select an NSC objective and a grade before choosing activities. Cover fractions, percentages or ratio where appropriate, with reverse and linked problems as extensions. Start with a short teacher reflection and an independent pupil example. Work through modelled examples and teacher challenges, apply one strategy in class, and revisit a comparable fresh question independently. Discuss explanations and misconceptions rather than comparing only scores. Initial/final reflections support professional learning, not a causal claim of impact. Agree any research participation, consent and use of findings separately. Do not collect pupil names in course reflections. Ministry sources checked 19 November 2026: https://moey.gov.jm/curricula/ and https://moey.gov.jm/changes-to-administration-of-pep-to-accommodate-students-impacted-by-hurricane-melissa/ . The latter describes 2026-specific changes. Do not assume its test dates, item counts or component arrangements apply to the next examination sitting. Confirm the current Ministry/school bulletin before giving assessment advice.

title: Your role in shaping the pilot

text: Your role in shaping the pilot
Kaizen Maths  /  Make It Count
Try one resource or strategy in your class
Note what helped and where pupils struggled
Report unclear content, errors or access problems
Suggest changes and useful classroom applications
What should we keep, change or develop next?

About 2 minutes. Agree a small first action: one resource or strategy, one grade and one lesson. Invite a short reflection with four prompts: What did you try? What helped? What was unclear or difficult? What should change? Ask for a description of the teaching situation so we learn where the approach can be effective. For software issues, ask for the page/tool, what the teacher tried, what happened and the device/browser if known. Keep screenshots free of pupil details, passwords and access codes. Agree a school contact, a feedback route and a check-in at the next session. Do not invent contact details or promise a particular feedback system. Close by asking: What should we keep, change or develop next? Explain that this feedback will help guide programme improvement and the software's development for wider use. No outcomes, dates or research permissions have been assumed.
